d.t: Beneath; below; at or to the bottom of, or the area covered or surmounted by.
d.e: We found some shade under a tree.

d.t: From one side of to the other, passing beneath.
d.e: I crawled under the fence.

d.t: Less than.
d.e: Interest rates are now under 1%.

d.t: Subject to.
d.e: We were constantly under bombardment.

d.t: Within the category, classification or heading of.
d.e: File this under "i" for "ignore".

d.t: (figuratively) In the face of; in response to (some attacking force).
d.e: to collapse under stress; to give in under interrogation

d.t: Using or adopting (a name, identity, etc.).
d.e: He writes books under the name John Smith.

d.t: In or to a lower or subordinate position, or a position beneath or below something, physically or figuratively.
d.e: pulled under by the currents

d.t: So as to pass beneath something.
d.e: There's quite a gap, so you may be able to sneak under.

d.t: (usually in compounds) Less than what is necessary to be adequate or suitable; insufficient.
d.e: The plants were underwatered.

d.t: (informal) In or into an unconscious state.
d.e: It took the hypnotist several minutes to make his subject go under.

d.t: Down to defeat, ruin, or death.
d.e: The COVID-19 epidemic and shutdown took some businesses under.

d.t: Lower; beneath something.
d.e: This treatment protects the under portion of the car from rust.

d.t: In a state of subordination, submission or defeat.
d.e: The army could not keep the people under.

d.t: (medicine, colloquial) Under anesthesia, especially general anesthesia; sedated.
d.e: Ensure the patient is sufficiently under.

d.t: (informal) Having a particular property that is low, especially so as to be insufficient or lacking in a particular respect.
d.e: This chicken is a bit under.

d.t: The amount by which an actual total is less than the expected or required amount.
(informal) Something having a particular property that is low or too low.
d.e: I went fishing but caught nothing but unders.

d.t: (gambling) A bet that a particular sporting statistic, such as points scored in a game, will be below a certain stated value.
(transitive, intransitive, of communication or means of communication: words, statements, signs, etc.) To know the meaning of; to parse or have parsed correctly; to comprehend.
d.e: Can you repeat what you just said? I didn't understand.

d.t: (transitive, of a skill, task, profession, etc.) To be thoroughly familiar with; to be able to undertake properly.
d.e: The students understood the assignment.

d.t: (transitive, usually with clause as object) To comprehend a fact or principle; to regard or come to regard a belief as such.
d.e: I understand that company policy says I can't get a refund, but can you make an exception?

d.t: (transitive, of people) To know the intent, motives or character of; (of events) to know the causes of or reasons for.
d.e: One day you say you love me, the next you ignore me—I don't understand you!

d.t: (transitive) To believe or infer, to think one grasps sufficiently despite potentially incomplete knowledge.
d.e: I've been given to understand that you have a package for me?

d.t: (transitive, grammar) To regard as present when not.
d.e: In the imperative mood, the word “you” is usually understood.

d.t: (humorous, rare, obsolete outside circus, acrobatics) To stand underneath, to support.
(Singapore, Malaysia, backchanneling) Uh-huh, I see; a way to acknowledge something said by the other speaker.
Indicating movement towards or location at a higher place or position.
Indicating movement in any other direction visualised as “up”.
To or in a position of equal advance or equality; not short of, back of, less advanced than, away from, etc.; usually followed by to or with.
d.e: I was up to my chin in water.

d.t: (intensifier) Used as an aspect marker to indicate a completed action or state; thoroughly, completely.
d.e: I will mix up the puzzle pieces.

d.t: To one's possession or consideration.
d.e: I picked up some milk on the way home.

d.t: From one's possession or consideration.
d.e: She had to give up her driver's license after the accident.

d.t: Aside or away, so as no longer to be present or in use.
d.e: to lay up riches; put up your weapons

d.t: (cricket) Relatively close to the batsman.
d.e: The bowler pitched the ball up.

d.t: (US, bartending) Without additional ice.
d.e: A Cosmopolitan is typically served up.

d.t: Toward the top of.
d.e: The cat climbed up the tree.

d.t: Toward the center, source, or main point of reference; toward the end at which something is attached.
d.e: The information made its way up the chain of command to the general.

d.t: From south to north of.
d.e: We sailed up the East Coast of England from Ipswich to South Shields.

d.t: Further along (in any direction).
d.e: Go up the street until you see the sign.

d.t: From the mouth towards the source of (a river or waterway).
d.e: He led an expedition up the Amazon.

d.t: (vulgar slang) Of a person: having sex with.
d.e: Phwoar, look at that bird. I'd love to be up her.

d.t: (colloquial) At (a given place, especially one imagined to be higher or more distant from a central location).
d.e: I'll see you later up the snooker club.

d.t: Facing upwards.
d.e: Turn the cloth over so that the patterned side is up.

d.t: On or at a physically higher level.
d.e: The flood waters are up again across large areas of the country.

d.t: Headed or designated to go upward (as an escalator, stairway, elevator etc.) or toward (as a run-up).
d.e: Where is the up escalator?

d.t: Fitted or fixed at a high or relatively high position, especially on a wall or ceiling.
d.e: All the notices are up now.

d.t: (by extension) Available to view or use; made public; posted.
d.e: Is your new video up yet? I looked on the website, but I couldn't find it.

d.t: Aloft.
d.e: The kite is up!

d.t: Raised; lifted.
d.e: The castle drawbridge was up.

d.t: (Australia) Of a river, in flood or at a high level.
Built, constructed.
d.e: Are the new buildings up yet?

d.t: Standing; upright.
d.e: The audience were up and on their feet.

d.t: (obsolete) Risen up, rebelling, in revolt.
Awake and out of bed.
d.e: I can’t believe it’s 3 a.m. and you’re still up.

d.t: (uncountable) The direction opposed to the pull of gravity.
d.e: Up is a good way to go.

d.t: (countable) A positive thing, or a time or situation when things are going well.
d.e: I hate almost everything about my job. The only up is that it's so close to home.

d.t: (particle physics) An up quark.
An upstairs room of a two story house.
d.e: She lives in a two-up two-down.

d.t: (transitive, poetic or in certain phrases) To physically raise or lift.
d.e: We upped anchor and sailed away.

d.t: (transitive, colloquial) To increase the level or amount of.
d.e: If we up the volume, we may be able to hear what he says.

d.t: (transitive, colloquial) To promote.
d.e: It wasn’t long before they upped him to Vice President.

d.t: (intransitive, often in combination with another verb) To rise to a standing position; hence, by extension, to act suddenly; see also up and.
d.e: She was sitting there quietly, then all of a sudden she upped and left.

d.t: (intransitive, archaic or poetic) To ascend; to climb up.
(computing, slang, transitive) To upload.
d.e: 100 new apps and games have just been upped.

d.t: (before the noun, idiomatic) Current; recent; the latest.
d.e: Use an up-to-date text for your source.

d.t: (idiomatic) Informed about the latest news or developments; abreast.
d.e: I like to stay up-to-date about current affairs.

d.t: Me and at least one other person, excluding the person(s) being addressed. (exclusive us.)
d.e: Don't treat us like idiots.

d.t: Me and at least one other person, including the person(s) being addressed. (inclusive us.)
d.e: Let's ask him if he'll give us a lift.

d.t: We, used in the same circumstances where “me” would be used instead of “I”, e.g. for the pronoun in isolation or as the complement of the copula:
d.e: Who's there? — Us. (or) — It's us.

d.t: Any entity that the speaker is a part of or identifies with, such as place of employment or education, nation, region, language, etc.
d.e: It's not true that the rest of Europe hates us.

d.t: People in general.
d.e: Grief ages us.

d.t: (colloquial) The person(s) being addressed.
d.e: Come on! Wakey wakey! Let's get us up and out of bed, please.

d.t: (colloquial) Used to imply connection between the speaker's experiences or activities and a group of listeners.
d.e: Hey guys, in this video I'll show you how I make my upside-down sponge cake. First let's get us a few ingredients that we'll need ...

d.t: (Commonwealth, colloquial, chiefly with certain verbs such as give, get, fetch, etc.) Me.
d.e: Give us a look at your paper.

d.t: (Northumbria) Me (in all contexts).
d.e: Look at us while ye’re speakin tiv us.

d.t: Designates the speaker(s)/writer(s) as constituting or belonging to the stated category of people (objective case).
d.e: It's not good enough for us teachers.

d.t: (proscribed) Designates the speaker(s)/writer(s) as constituting or belonging to the stated category of people (subjective case).
(Northern England, Nottinghamshire) Our.
d.e: We'll have to throw us food out.

d.t: (informal) The relationship between the speaker and some other unspecified person.
d.e: There is no us.

d.t: (rare) Alternative form of u's.
The act of using.
d.e: The use of torture has been condemned by the United Nations.

d.t: (uncountable) The act of consuming alcohol or narcotics.
(uncountable, followed by of) Usefulness, utility, benefit; purpose, point.
d.e: Near-synonyms: meaning, meaningfulness

d.t: A function; a purpose for which something may be employed.
d.e: This tool has many uses.

d.t: Occasion or need to employ; necessity.
d.e: I have no further use for these textbooks, but we may have use for all these other things later.

d.t: (obsolete, rare) Interest for lent money; premium paid for the use of something; usury.
(archaic) Continued or repeated practice; usage; habit.
(obsolete) Common occurrence; ordinary experience.
(Christianity) A special form of a rite adopted for use in a particular context, often a diocese.
d.e: the Sarum, or Canterbury, use; the York use; the Ordinariate use

d.t: (forging) A slab of iron welded to the side of a forging, such as a shaft, near the end, and afterward drawn down, by hammering, so as to lengthen the forging.
To utilize or employ.
To accustom; to habituate. (Now common only in participial form. Uses the same pronunciation as the noun; see usage notes.)
d.e: soldiers who are used to hardships and danger

d.t: (intransitive, archaic or literary except in past tense) To habitually do; to be wont to do. (Now chiefly in past-tense forms; see used to.)
d.e: I used to get things done.

d.t: (dated) To behave toward; to act with regard to; to treat.
d.e: to use an animal cruelly

d.t: (reflexive, obsolete) To behave, act, comport oneself.
d.e:
1551, Thomas More, Utopia, London: B. Alsop & T. Fawcet, 1639, “Of Bond-men, Sicke persons, Wedlocke, and divers other matters,” page 231,
They live together lovingly: For no Magistrate is either haughty or fearefull. Fathers they be called, and like fathers they use themselves.

d.t: (of a resource) To consume, deplete, expend, or exhaust.
(of time or space) To take or occupy.
(chiefly computing) Designed to be easy for an untrained user to use, with intuitive ordering of steps, consistent and logical placement of controls, etc.
Most of the time; less than always, but more than occasionally.
d.e: Except for one or two days a year, he usually walks to work.

d.t: Under normal conditions.
